rv.q: I don't blame Wanted for taking the way of most enjoyment in its telling of Mary and Martha's story.
This messiness is a shame because a great musical could yet be somewhere inside this odd contraption.
The end result is spirited but uneven, a show wherein some very big singing nearly succeeds in drowning out needling plot contrivances and characterizations as thin as a wanted poster.
Add in a less-than-riveting performance from James, who has weak sauce to work with, and 'Wanted' ultimately falls off what initially looked like very promising rails.
As a Broadway show, however, it simply doesn't measure up.
As is, this is a western that’s not wild enough, a melodrama lacking heat, a song showcase that grows repetitive in all its smooth and unsurprising melody.

At every step, the Broadway show by Ross Baum and Angelica Chéri squanders what’s good about it — namely an enticing premise and a cast of powerful singers — and instead churns out a gaudy, uninvolving slog in which plot movements are at the same time bonkers and blasé.
You’ll cheer for the Clarke sisters robbing oppressive white society in post-Reconstruction Marlin, Texas in Wanted , now on Broadway under the direction of Stevie Walker-Webb.
Flawed as it may be, Wanted has a winning quality that constantly breaks through.
This is the Wanted that has the power to shake up Broadway: the show that delivers the powerful truth that no matter the path to freedom you choose, it inevitably comes with a catastrophic blast.
Too many of the two dozen musical numbers in “Wanted” force the show’s first-rate singers to start full-throttle and rarely dip into a more moderate register.
That Wanted tries to give us all three frustratingly dilutes the overall production.
As brilliant a job as he’s done with casting the show, director Stevie Walker-Webb could have done a sharper job of shaping and structuring “Wanted.”

Neatly meshing effective performances and terrific singing with excellent visuals, Stevie Walker-Webb, the director, delivers Wanted as a solid Broadway production that looks as good as it sounds in Beowulf Boritt’s handsome scenic design.
Sadly, the frequently disjointed final product too often feels like a victim of overdevelopment.
Wanted has got a lot of hits and misses.
Several songs begin small and promisingly, but after a stanza or two, the tunes inevitably go big and quickly crescendo into deafening.
But despite the tantalizing promises the Kinfolk make, Wanted ’s overdramatic, self-serious script and under-dramatic score prevent the show from living up to its refreshingly audacious ambitions.
Gifted singers and a gospel-inflected score can’t overcome a production that specializes in overkill and silliness.
A few counterfeit bills may turn up in those bags of cash, but in an era of revivals and cash-cow adaptations, Wanted is still worth the bounty.
For all its flaws, Wanted earns its place in the spotlight — and challenges us to consider why we still call the Midtown theater district the Great White Way.
Wanted is fast-paced, fabulous and absolutely worth fawning over.

cn.t: Critics find this original musical about outlaw sisters overly ambitious and uneven, though they consistently praise the powerhouse vocals and explosive singing that nearly compensate for a flawed script and thin characterizations.

vs.sum: A beautifully restored theater with a stunning Tiffany-inspired interior. The 2021 renovation transformed restroom facilities from among Broadway's worst to a model for the industry, with modern bathrooms on every public level.

acc.note: Elevator to Mezzanine, Balcony, and lower level restrooms. 7 wheelchair spaces across all levels.
